theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is a quotation?
options: A rough guess of the price that may change a lot
A bill sent to the customer after the work is finished
A written offer to do stated work for a stated price
A list of the hours each worker spent on a job

questions.stem: How is an estimate different from a quotation?
options: An estimate is an approximate price; a quotation is a firm price
An estimate is always a higher price than the quotation would be
An estimate is only ever given for electrical work, not welding
An estimate must be signed by a lawyer before it is sent

questions.stem: Before you work out a price for a job, what must you be clear about first?
options: Exactly what work the customer wants done
How much money the customer earns each month
How much the last customer paid
Which worker is free next week

questions.stem: Why is a site visit often needed before quoting for a gate or for rewiring a room?
options: To meet the customer's family and neighbours
To start the work before the price is agreed
To collect a deposit before the quote is written
To measure and see any problems that affect the price

questions.stem: A window opening is 1200 mm wide and 1500 mm high. What is its area?
options: 2.7 m²
1.8 m²
18 m²

questions.stem: A rectangular steel frame is 2 m long and 1 m wide. How much tube is needed for the outside of the frame? (Ignore waste.)
options: 2 m
3 m
6 m
4 m

questions.stem: Steel tube is sold in 6 m lengths. A job needs 14 m of tube. How many lengths must you price?
options: 2 lengths
3 lengths
4 lengths
14 lengths

questions.stem: Why is an allowance for waste added to the material quantities?
options: So that the worker can take extra material home
Because suppliers always deliver short
To make the quote look bigger than the others
Offcuts, cutting and mistakes use extra material

questions.stem: A room needs 5 socket outlets. Each one needs a box, a socket and two fixing screws. How many fixing screws should be priced?
Cable costs J$250 per metre. The job needs 40 m. What is the cost of the cable?
Where should you get up-to-date material prices for a quotation?
options: From an old price list that you kept from two years ago
From what a friend paid for a similar job
By guessing and adding a little extra
From current supplier price lists or written quotes

questions.stem: Two suppliers give prices for the same steel. What else should you compare, besides the price?
options: Which supplier has the biggest shop and car park
Quality, delivery time and stock available
How far their shop is from your own home
Which one has the brightest sign out front

questions.stem: Two workers will each work 8 hours on a job. The labour rate is J$1,200 per hour for each worker. What is the labour cost?
How can you best judge how many hours a job will take?
options: Use records of similar jobs and ask experienced workers
Pick a number that makes the price look low
Always allow one day, whatever the job is
Ask the customer how long they think it should take you

questions.stem: Which cost is often forgotten when pricing a job away from the workshop?
options: Transport and travel to the site
The main materials on the drawing
The hours of the main work
The parts listed by the customer

questions.stem: In a welding job, which items are consumables (used up during the job) that should be included in the price?
options: The welding machine and the grinder
The workshop roof and the bench
The company van and its tyres
Electrodes, grinding discs and gas

questions.stem: What are overheads?
options: The cost of materials for one job
Running costs such as rent and electricity
Extra money paid by the customer for fast work
The profit the owner takes home

questions.stem: The total costs for a job are J$50,000. The business adds a 20% markup for profit. What is the price before tax?
Why must a business include profit in its prices?
options: So that it can grow, replace tools and stay in business
So that its price is always the highest in town
Because the law says every job must make a 50% profit
So that its workers do not need to be paid wages

questions.stem: Many businesses in Jamaica must add GCT to their prices. How should it be shown on a quotation?
options: Hidden inside the labour cost
Left off and added to the bill later as a surprise
Shown as a separate line at the current rate
Added only if the customer asks about it

questions.stem: Materials cost J$35,000, labour costs J$24,000 and transport costs J$4,000. What is the subtotal?
Which detail must a quotation always show?
options: The customer's date of birth
The worker's home address
A clear description of the work to be done
The supplier's own private mobile phone number

questions.stem: Why should each quotation have its own number and date?
options: So that it can be found and matched to the job later
So that the customer knows how old the worker is
So that the price can be changed each day
So that it looks more official, like a bank statement

questions.stem: A quotation says "Valid for 30 days". What does this mean?
options: The work will take 30 days to finish
The customer must pay within 30 days
The price can be accepted within 30 days
The warranty on the work lasts 30 days

questions.stem: Why does a quotation have a time limit?
options: The customer may move house soon
The paper copy may fade in the sun
The worker may forget about the job
Material prices can change over time

questions.stem: Why do many small businesses ask for a deposit before starting a large job?
options: To help buy materials and confirm the order
To pay the workers a bonus before they start
Because a deposit means no quote is needed
So that the customer cannot ask for changes

questions.stem: A quote for rewiring a house says "Excludes plastering and painting". Why is this written on it?
options: So that the electrician can charge for it twice
So that the customer knows what is not in the price
Because plastering is never needed after rewiring
To make the quotation look longer and more official

questions.stem: What are the payment terms on a quotation?
options: The words used to thank the customer
The list of tools that will be used
When and how the customer must pay
The names of the workers on the job

questions.stem: Before a quotation is sent, what should be checked?
options: Only the spelling of the customer's name
The colour of the paper it is printed on
The style of letters used in the heading
The quantities, prices and all the sums

questions.stem: Delroy is a junior worker and has priced a job. What should he do before the quote is sent?
options: Send it at once so that the customer gets it quickly
Ask his supervisor to check and approve it
Lower the price so that the customer says yes
Leave out the labour so that it looks cheaper

questions.stem: What can happen if a job is priced too low?
options: The customer will always refuse to accept it
The materials will cost the business less
The business may lose money doing the job
The work will be done much faster

questions.stem: What can happen if a job is priced much too high?
options: The customer may go to another business
The business will lose money on the job
The supplier will lower its prices
The job will take longer to finish

questions.stem: When you give a quotation to a customer, what is good practice?
options: Hand it over and leave without speaking
Explain each part and answer their questions
Tell them that they must decide today
Say the price is too high to discuss

questions.stem: A customer says your quote is higher than one from another business. What is the best reply?
options: Tell them the other business is cheating
Cut your price in half straight away
Tell them to go with the other business, then
Explain what your price includes and why

questions.stem: How should a customer show that they accept a quotation?
options: By telling a neighbour they are happy
By paying the full price before any work
By not replying for a month
By signing and dating the acceptance part

questions.stem: During the job, the customer asks for two extra window grills. What should you do?
options: Agree the extra work and price in writing first
Fit them and add them to the bill without saying
Refuse, because the quote cannot be changed
Fit them for free to keep the customer happy

questions.stem: While rewiring a house, an electrician finds old wiring in a wall that is damaged and must be replaced. It was not in the quote. What should happen?
options: Do the work and add it to the bill quietly
Cover it up again and finish the rest of the job as quoted
Explain it to the customer and agree the extra cost
Stop work and leave without explaining

questions.stem: Why should a copy of every quotation be kept?
options: To give to other customers as a sample
To check the price when the job is done and billed
So that the price on it can be changed later on if needed
To show the bank how busy you are

questions.stem: A customer has not replied to a quote after a week. What should you do?
options: Send them the bill for the job anyway
Contact them politely to ask if they have questions
Turn up and start the job to show them that you are keen
Throw the quote away and forget the job

questions.stem: Why should your business's costings and price lists be kept private?
options: So that customers never know what they pay
So that the tax office cannot check them
So that workers cannot see their wages
So that competitors cannot undercut your prices

questions.stem: A customer is offered a 5% discount on a J$40,000 job. How much is the discount?
A job needs a scaffold tower that the business does not own. How should this be priced?
options: Ask the customer to build one
Leave it out and borrow one
Include the hire cost in the quotation
Stand on a chair or a drum instead to save money

questions.stem: Each of 4 window grills needs 9 m of 12 mm square bar. How many metres are needed in total, before waste?
A quote says "Labour: 3 days". Why is it better to also say what work is included?
options: So that the workers can take longer if needed
Because days are not a proper unit of time
So that the price can be raised during the job
So the customer knows what they are paying for

questions.stem: How should a written quotation look?
options: Handwritten in pencil on scrap paper
Neat, clear and on the business's letterhead or form
Typed in capital letters with no headings
Sent only as a voice note, with no written copy at all

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What do the letters GCT stand for?
What is the name for working out a list of all the materials and quantities from a drawing?
A quotation total is J$80,000 and the customer must pay a 50% deposit. How much is the deposit, in Jamaican dollars?
You measure a gap as 2.5 m. How many millimetres is that?
What is the name for an agreed change to the work after a quotation has been accepted?
What do we call a business that sells materials to your business?
A job costs the business J$30,000 and the customer pays J$36,000. How much profit is made, in Jamaican dollars?
Materials for a job cost J$45,000. You add 10% for waste. How much is the waste allowance, in Jamaican dollars?
What is the name for a formal offer to price a large job, often sent in against other businesses by a closing date?
Which measuring tool would you take on a site visit to measure a window opening?
A price list shows cable at "J$250 per m". What does "per m" mean?
What is the name for a computer program with rows and columns that is often used to work out the costs for a quote?
A job needs 3 workers for 2 days, working 8 hours each day. How many worker-hours is that?
A job needs 4 runs of conduit, each 3.5 m long. How many metres of conduit is that in total, before waste?
When a customer signs to accept a quotation, what kind of agreement is made between the customer and the business?

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to prepare a quotation, from the customer's first enquiry to sending the quote.
essays.modelAnswer: First I talk to the customer and find out exactly what they want, when they need it and any budget. If needed, I visit the site to measure and look for anything that affects the job, such as access or old wiring. I make a sketch with the sizes. From the sketch or drawing I work out the materials and quantities, add a waste allowance and get current prices from suppliers. I work out the labour hours and cost, and add other costs such as consumables, transport and equipment hire. I add the markup for overheads and profit, then any tax at the current rate, to get the total. I write the quotation on the business form with the description of the work, prices, validity, payment terms and exclusions. I check all the figures, get my supervisor to approve it, send it and keep a copy.
markingPoints: Finds out the customer's needs, timing and budget
Visits the site, measures and sketches
Works out materials with waste, labour and other costs using current prices
Adds markup and tax to reach the total
Writes the quote with terms, checks it, gets approval, sends it and keeps a copy

essays.stem: Describe what you would look for and record on a site visit before quoting for steel window grills or for adding sockets and lights to a room.
essays.modelAnswer: I arrive on time, introduce myself and ask the customer to show me exactly what they want. I measure each window or wall carefully with a tape, at least twice, and write the sizes on a sketch, numbering each window or position. I check the condition of the walls and frames, because weak blocks or rotten frames change the fixings and the work needed. For electrical work, I note where the supply and the distribution board are, the cable routes, the wall type, and whether the existing wiring looks old or damaged, but I do not open live equipment. I look at the access: parking, stairs, height and whether a ladder or scaffold is needed. I note any safety issues, such as children, pets or a busy road. I take photos with the customer's permission and confirm the main details with the customer before I leave.
markingPoints: Confirms what the customer wants
Measures carefully, twice, and records sizes on a numbered sketch
Checks wall, frame or wiring condition and fixing needs (without opening live equipment)
Notes access, height and equipment needed, and safety issues
Takes photos with permission and confirms details with the customer

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out the cost of materials for a quotation.
essays.modelAnswer: I start from the drawing or my site sketch and make a take-off list of every item, with its size and quantity, such as lengths of square tube, flat bar, hinges and bolts for a gate, or boxes, sockets, cable and conduit for electrical work. I work out the total length of each section and turn it into the number of stock lengths or rolls the supplier sells, always rounding up. I add a waste allowance for offcuts and cutting. I also list consumables that are easy to forget, such as electrodes, grinding discs, gas, paint, fixings and cable ties. Then I get current prices from supplier price lists or written quotes, and compare suppliers on price, quality and delivery time. I multiply each quantity by its price and add them up, using a spreadsheet or calculator, and check the sums twice.
markingPoints: Makes a take-off list of every item, size and quantity
Converts to stock lengths or rolls, rounding up
Adds a waste allowance and includes consumables and fixings
Uses current supplier prices and compares suppliers
Multiplies, totals and checks the sums

essays.stem: Explain how you would work out the labour cost and the other costs, apart from materials, for a quotation.
essays.modelAnswer: To work out labour, I break the job into tasks, such as cutting, welding, grinding, painting and fitting, or chasing walls, running cable, fixing boxes, connecting and testing. I estimate the hours for each task, using records of similar jobs and advice from experienced workers, and I add time for travel, setting up and cleaning up. I multiply the hours by the number of workers and by the labour rate, for example 2 workers × 8 hours × J$1,200 = J$19,200. Then I add the other costs. These include transport to and from the site, hire of equipment such as a scaffold tower or generator, any permits, and special PPE. The business's overheads, such as rent, electricity, insurance and tool wear, must also be covered, either in the labour rate or in the markup. Leaving these out means the business loses money.
markingPoints: Breaks the job into tasks and estimates hours from records and experience
Adds travel, set-up and clean-up time
Calculates hours × workers × rate correctly
Adds transport, equipment hire and other direct costs
Covers overheads in the rate or the markup

essays.stem: Explain why a business adds a markup to its costs, and what can go wrong if a job is priced too low or too high.
essays.modelAnswer: The costs of a job are the materials, labour and other direct costs. A markup is an extra amount, often a percentage of the costs, that is added to pay for the business's overheads and to give a profit. For example, if the costs are J$50,000 and the markup is 20%, the price before tax is J$60,000. The profit lets the business pay for new tools and machines, cover slow months and bad debts, and grow. If a job is priced too low, the business may not cover its costs and will lose money, and it may have to cut corners, which can lead to poor or unsafe work. If a job is priced much too high, the customer may go to another business and the work is lost. A fair price covers all costs and a reasonable profit, and matches the quality offered.
markingPoints: Explains a markup as an amount added to costs
Markup covers overheads and gives a profit
Gives a correct worked example
Too low: losses and cut corners
Too high: the customer goes elsewhere; aim for a fair price

essays.stem: Describe the information that should appear on a written quotation.
essays.modelAnswer: The quotation should be on the business's letterhead or form, with the business name, address, phone number and any tax registration number. It should have its own quotation number and the date. It shows the customer's name, address and contact details, and the job address if it is different. It gives a clear description of the work, for example "Make and fit 4 window grills from 12 mm square bar, primed and painted black". The prices are set out item by item or in sections, such as materials, labour and other costs, with a subtotal, any tax at the current rate and the total. The terms are given: how long the price is valid, the deposit and payment terms, the expected start and finish dates, what is not included, and the warranty. It ends with the name and signature of the person issuing it and a space for the customer to sign their acceptance.
markingPoints: Business details, quotation number and date
Customer and job address details
Clear description of the work
Itemised prices, subtotal, tax and total
Terms (validity, payment, dates, exclusions, warranty) and signatures

essays.stem: Explain why a quotation should include terms such as how long it is valid, the deposit, payment terms, exclusions and the warranty.
essays.modelAnswer: The terms make it clear what both the business and the customer are agreeing to, so that there are fewer arguments later. The validity period, such as 30 days, protects the business because material prices can rise; after that time the price may be checked again. A deposit helps the business buy the materials and shows that the customer is serious about the job. The payment terms say when the balance must be paid and how, for example on completion by bank transfer, so the customer is not surprised. Exclusions list what is not in the price, such as plastering after rewiring or painting a gate, so the customer knows what they must arrange themselves. The warranty says how long the work is guaranteed and what it covers, which gives the customer confidence. Clear terms are fair to both sides.
markingPoints: Terms make the agreement clear and prevent disputes
Validity: protects against price changes
Deposit and payment terms: buying materials, when and how to pay
Exclusions: what is not included
Warranty: what is guaranteed and for how long

essays.stem: Describe how you would check a quotation before it is sent to the customer.
essays.modelAnswer: I check that the description of the work matches what the customer asked for and what I measured on site. I check the take-off list against the drawing or sketch to make sure no item has been missed, such as fixings, consumables or transport. I check each quantity and each price, making sure the prices are current. I check every sum, either by working it out again or by asking someone else to check it, including the markup, the subtotal, any tax and the total. I check the terms: the validity period, deposit, payment terms, start date, exclusions and warranty. I check the customer's name, address and contact details, the quote number and the date, and the spelling. Then I give it to my supervisor to approve and sign. Only then is it sent, and a copy is filed.
markingPoints: Description matches the customer's request and the site measurements
Take-off checked for missing items
Quantities, prices and all sums checked again
Terms, customer details, number, date and spelling checked
Supervisor approves before sending; a copy is filed

essays.stem: Describe how you would present a quotation to a customer and deal with their questions, and what you would do afterwards.
essays.modelAnswer: I give the quotation in person, by email or by message, as the customer prefers, and offer to go through it. I explain the work that is included, the materials, the price and the terms in plain words, and point out what is not included. I listen to the customer's questions and answer honestly. If they think the price is high, I explain what it includes, such as the quality of the materials, the warranty and safe work, and I may offer a cheaper option, such as a simpler design, but I do not cut corners on safety. If they ask for a discount I cannot give, I ask my supervisor. I tell the customer how long the price is valid and how to accept it. Afterwards I record the date it was sent, and if I hear nothing after about a week, I contact them politely to ask if they have any questions.
markingPoints: Offers to go through the quote and explains it in plain words
Points out exclusions and terms
Answers questions honestly and explains the value; offers options without unsafe cuts
Refers discounts beyond their authority to the supervisor
Records the date sent and follows up politely

essays.stem: Explain what you should do if a customer asks for extra work, or if you find a problem that was not in the quotation, after the job has started.
essays.modelAnswer: I should not just do the extra work and add it to the bill, and I should not ignore a problem. If the customer asks for extra work, such as two more window grills or an extra outside light, I explain that it is not in the quotation. I work out the extra materials, labour and time, and give the customer a written price for the change, called a variation. If I find a problem, such as damaged old wiring or a rotten door frame, I stop that part of the work if it is unsafe, show the customer and explain why it must be dealt with and what it will cost. In both cases I tell my supervisor, and I only go ahead when the customer has agreed the change and the price in writing. I record the variation with the job papers so that the final bill matches what was agreed.
markingPoints: Does not do unpriced extra work or ignore a problem
Explains to the customer that it is outside the quote
Prices the change in writing as a variation
Tells the supervisor and gets the customer's written agreement before going ahead
Records the variation so the bill matches

practical1.title: Measure a job at the Centre and prepare a costing sheet
practical1.brief: The assessor chooses a job at the Centre for your group to price, for example steel burglar-bar grills for a classroom window, or adding four socket outlets and two lights to a room. As a group, act as if the Centre is your customer. Measure the job on site, at least twice, and make a neat sketch with the sizes. Then make a take-off list of every material, change it into stock lengths or rolls, and add a waste allowance. Use the price list the assessor gives you to cost the materials, consumables and fixings. Work out the labour hours and labour cost at the rate on the price list, add transport and any equipment hire, then add the markup the assessor gives you. Share the work so that each member does one part of the costing sheet and checks another member's sums, initialling each check. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in the sketch and the costing sheet once for the whole group.
materials: A job chosen by the assessor at the Centre
5 m tape measures, pencils, clipboards and squared paper
A supplier price list and a labour rate from the assessor
A blank costing sheet (on paper or in a spreadsheet)
A step stool only if the assessor allows it
photos: The group measuring the job on site
The finished sketch with all sizes
The take-off list with stock lengths and waste allowance
The materials and labour parts of the costing sheet
Members checking each other's sums, with initials on the sheet
The finished costing sheet showing the total before tax
checklist: Measured accurately, twice, and recorded the sizes clearly
Helped make a neat sketch with all the sizes needed
Listed every material, fixing and consumable with the right quantity
Rounded up to stock lengths or rolls and added a waste allowance
Used the price list and labour rate correctly
Added transport, hire and the markup correctly
Checked another member's sums and corrected any mistake
Worked well with the group and kept the paperwork neat
safety: Measure from the floor; use a step stool only if the assessor allows it, and never stand on chairs or desks
Do not open sockets, switches or the distribution board; measure electrical positions from the outside only
Keep tape measures under control so that they do not snap back and cut you

practical2.title: Write and present a quotation to a customer
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a job brief with a finished costing, for a job different from Practical 1, such as a steel handrail for the front steps of a villa, or four outdoor security lights for a shop. As a group, write a full quotation on a quotation form or in a word processor. Use a made-up business name and details. Include the quotation number, date, customer details, a clear description of the work, itemised prices, the subtotal, GCT at the rate the assessor gives you, the total, how long the price is valid, the deposit and payment terms, start and finish dates, exclusions, the warranty and a space for the customer to sign. Check it and have it approved by your "supervisor" (the assessor). Then present it to a "customer" played by the assessor or another member: each member explains one part, and the group answers the customer's questions, including a request for one extra item, which you must price as a variation. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: The job brief and finished costing from the assessor
Blank quotation forms, or a computer with a word processor or spreadsheet
The supplier price list (for pricing the variation)
A table and chairs set up as an office
photos: The finished quotation, showing the itemised prices and total
The terms part of the quotation (validity, payment, exclusions, warranty)
The quotation being checked and approved by the supervisor
Members presenting the quotation to the customer
The priced variation and the customer's signed acceptance
checklist: Wrote a clear description of the work that matches the brief
Set out itemised prices, subtotal, GCT and total correctly
Included validity, deposit, payment terms, dates, exclusions and warranty
Checked the figures and details before approval
Explained their part of the quotation clearly, in plain words
Answered the customer's questions politely and honestly
Priced the extra item correctly as a variation and got it agreed in writing
Took a fair share of the writing and the presenting
safety: Use only made-up business and customer details
Sit at the computer with good posture and take short breaks from the screen
Keep cables from the computer and chargers out of walkways
Take photos only with the permission of everyone in them
